input.description: Guard: refs de respaldo antes de mover ramas
input.prompt:
Build a mechanism so that a worker dying mid-history-rewrite can never leave its commits reachable only through the reflog. (A previous worker on this errand could not be resumed because its worktree was never created on disk. Nothing of it exists, so start clean.)

MEASURED (by me, 2026-09-15):
- A worker replaying its branch onto develop reset branch `worktree-agent-a153f28c32544646b` to 9f282737 (reflog entry "branch: Reset to 9f282737"), then hit a session limit and died.
- Its 11 commits (706a4b74..ebf3cf88) were left reachable ONLY from the reflog, which is GC-eligible. I saved them by hand with `git update-ref refs/backup/a11y-a153-2026-09-14 ebf3cf88`.
- Earlier, a `git branch -D` left a commit dangling in the same way.
- `git rebase` is denied to workers by permissions, so they emulate it with reset + cherry-pick. That emulation is the risky window.

HYPOTHESIS: the root is that any command that moves a branch ref to a point not containing its current tip (or deletes the branch) drops commits from every ref, and nothing records them first.
- One option: a PreToolUse hook on Bash|PowerShell that detects ref-moving commands (`git reset`, `git branch -f/-D/-M`, `git checkout -B`, `git switch -C`, `git update-ref`) and, BEFORE they run, writes `refs/backup/<branch>/<timestamp>` at the current tip whenever that tip is not contained in the target.
- The alternative is to refuse the command unless such a backup exists.
- Decide which is right and state the tradeoffs: a hook cannot run after the command, and refusing blocks legitimate replays.

BUILD in your worktree's .claude/ (gitignored; nothing enters git). Worktree isolation will refuse writes to the main checkout, so do NOT route around it.
- The hook.
- A selftest.mjs over CONSTRUCTED throwaway repos covering at least:
  - tip contained in the target (no backup needed);
  - tip not contained (a backup is made and resolves to the old tip);
  - branch delete;
  - non-git commands;
  - the tokens appearing as DATA (heredoc, echo, commit message);
  - commands run in worktrees;
  - PowerShell payload shape.
- A `list` command that reports backup refs whose commits are not on develop, so they get triaged instead of piling up.
- An idempotent install script (`--dry-run` supported) that copies the files into the main checkout's .claude/ and registers the hook in .claude/settings.local.json, backing that file up first and printing everything it does.

Report: files, selftest count, the design decision with tradeoffs, and the install command. I will read the code and run the install plus a real-payload proof from the main session.

input.description: Quality gate for honest component output typing
input.prompt:
You are building a quality gate for @base100/b100-am-ui (Angular 19 library). The contract in `.claude/AGENT-LEDGER.md` binds you. Read it first if its heading is not in your context. All `.claude/` tooling lives only in the main checkout, so always call it by absolute path: `C:/Users/adrian.jimenez/Desktop/Projects/b100-am-ui/.claude/...`. Never change worktree, never `git rebase`, never `npm install` in your worktree.

GOAL (owner directive): the next time a component's public types lie, a gate fails. It must not depend on a reviewer noticing.

The defect class, from three real incidents this week:
1. Over-wide outputs. `B100ButtonToggleComponent.valueChange` was `output<T[] | T>()` whatever `multiple` was. `B100InputComponent.valueChange` was `output<string | number | null>()` for every `config.type`. Consumers had to handle arms they could never receive.
2. Casts instead of types. A demo worker "fixed" (1) with lying `as` casts in consumer code and turned off `@typescript-eslint/non-nullable-type-assertion-style` project-wide (rejected and reverted). Then a library fix typed `valueChange` generically but emitted through `value as B100InputValueOf<C>`, plus a default `input<C>({} as C)`.
3. Two sources of truth for a discriminant. b100-input still has an inline `type` input that overrides `config.type`, so the generic type computed from the config is unsound.

MEASURED (by me, reading branch worktree-agent-ad29a95bc2ed88cb0 at 9e19ce53): `src/lib/components/b100-input/b100-input.component.ts` has `readonly type = input<...>()` at :135, `readonly config = input<C>({} as C)` at :126, and `this.valueChange.emit(value as B100InputValueOf<C>)` at :391.
MEASURED (by me): commit 3c2d4899 on branch integrate/spec-typecheck-a splits button-toggle into `valueChange: T` and `valuesChange: readonly T[]`, routed by a real type guard with no cast.
HYPOTHESIS (unverified, settle it with the tools): `@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-assertions` with `assertionStyle: 'never'` (const assertions stay allowed) can ban value-level `as` in `src/lib/**`. How many offenders exist today is unknown. Measure it with `eslint --print-config` plus a real run, never a grep count.
HYPOTHESIS: face 3 needs a custom rule in the repo's own plugin, `tools/b100-eslint-plugin`, using type information. It would flag a component class that declares both a `config` input whose type is a union (or Partial of a union) discriminated by a literal-typed property, and a separate `input()` with the same name as that discriminant.

WHAT TO DO:
1. THINK FIRST. For each face, write down what property the gate decides, which tool owns that question (ESLint core, a typescript-eslint rule, a custom type-aware rule, or a `check:*` script), and what would make the gate wrong: false positives on legitimate code such as `as const` or `satisfies`, and false negatives on the real incidents above.
2. MEASURE the current population in lib, demo and consumer-app per face, with the owning tool. List every offender with file:line.
3. BUILD the mechanism with the best architecture available: prefer existing official rules, and write a custom rule only where no official one decides the property. Each custom rule gets RuleTester tests covering the whole state space, including near misses: the three real incidents reproduced as fixtures, `as const`, `satisfies`, a legitimate generic default without a cast, and a component with an inline override that is NOT a discriminant. It also gets bilingual docs matching the plugin's existing rule docs.
4. ENABLE ONLY AT ZERO. Owner rule, `failure-hidden-in-a-central-exception-registry`: no suppressions file, no baseline, no ignore list, no per-file `off`. If the offenders are in your reach, fix them at the root with typed APIs, the way 3c2d4899 did, not with casts. Do NOT touch b100-input: worker ad29a95 is fixing it. It is a live, owned file, so leave it and report it as the known offender. If offenders remain, register the rule but do NOT enable it, and report the exact list.
5. Prove each rule DISCRIMINATES: re-introduce one real incident on a scratch copy, show the gate goes red, revert it, show it goes green. Paste both runs.
6. Verification, with exit codes: `npm run typecheck`, `npm run lint`, `npm run format:check`, `npm run build:demo`, the plugin's own test suite, and `npx jiti scripts/test/test.ts --project lib`. If the plugin is consumed through a `file:` package, confirm your gates resolve YOUR copy.
7. Everything bilingual (English + `@es`), commits in English Conventional form with no attribution. Commit before reporting.

Report: commits, the file list, each face with its owning tool and why, the measured population, the discrimination proof, and which rules are enabled versus registered-but-pending with their offender lists.

WHAT THE HUNK DOES: a push publishing no commits (a deletion-only push, where `b100_pushed_local_shas` drops git's all-zero local shas) exits 0 before `--verify-trees`, because removing a ref from the server cannot introduce a red and charging it a full local verification is cost for zero information.

YOUR JOB:
1. Land that hunk as a commit, with a test that proves the early exit DISCRIMINATES rather than merely runs. Enumerate the state space the decision ranges over and exercise each state: a deletion-only push takes the early exit; a normal push does NOT and still reaches `--verify-trees`; and the NEAR MISS — a push plan mixing a deletion with a real ref update — must NOT take the early exit. A guard proven only to fire is not a guard proven to decide.
2. Prove your test can go RED: mutate the early exit (e.g. make it unconditional), run the test, and report exactly which assertions fail and that the others do not. A test suite that stays green under a mutation of the thing it tests is measuring your execution order, not the code.

There is precedent for a zero-dep `.mjs` selftest — see `.claude/fleet-env/reap.selftest.mjs` — and precedent for a vitest spec under `scripts/**/testing/`.
